report.source_text: Moreover, NGS was conducted from a piece of alveolar process and adjacent mucous membrane. Following DNA extraction, DNA libraries were constructed and sequenced by the MGISEQ-2000 platform [8]. High-quality sequencing data were generated by removing low-quality reads, followed by computational subtraction of human host sequences mapped to the human reference genome (hg19) using Burrows‒Wheeler Alignment [9]. The remaining data obtained by removal of low-complexity reads were classified by simultaneous alignment to the Pathogens Metagenomics Database (PMDB), consisting of bacteria, fungi, viruses and parasites. Finally, Prevotella, Streptococcus, Lactobacillus, Veillonella, Actinomyces, Candida, VZV, HBV, human gammaherpesvirus 4 and Torque teno virus (TTV) were detected by NGS. Thus, the coexistence of bacterial and viral infection was confirmed.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 67-year-old man presented with a 5-week history of facial erythema, clustered blisters, and pain, initially diagnosed as Herpes Zoster (HZ) by a stomatologist 4 weeks prior. He received antiviral treatment. Subsequently, he developed severe toothache and exfoliation of four teeth in the upper right jaw. Clinical examination revealed pigmentation and scars on the right face, and intraoral examination showed exposed alveolar process, loss of crowns, and residual roots in the maxillary arch. Imaging studies (panoramic radiography and CT) confirmed decreased bone density, poor alveolar socket healing, and empty tooth sockets in the right maxilla. Biopsy of the affected tissue revealed nonvital lamellar bone, vascular necrosis, and inflammation. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) of the alveolar process and mucous membrane detected Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV), along with bacterial co-infection, confirming the presence of VZV in the osteonecrotic tissue and supporting the diagnosis of alveolar osteonecrosis following facial HZ.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with symptoms consistent with facial HZ (erythema, clustered blisters, great pain in the right face) and was initially diagnosed with HZ.
Patient developed severe toothache and exfoliation of four teeth in the upper right jaw, indicating bone involvement.
Extraoral examination showed pigmentation and scars on the right half of the face, consistent with resolved HZ lesions.
Intraoral examination revealed exposed alveolar process, complete loss of crowns, and residual roots in the maxillary arch, indicative of significant bone and dental damage.
Panoramic radiography showed decreased bone density and poor alveolar socket healing in the right maxilla, while CT revealed empty tooth sockets, consistent with alveolar osteonecrosis.

Histopathological examination of the affected tissue showed fragments of nonvital lamellar bone devoid of osteoblasts and osteocytes, surrounded by neutrophils and bacterial aggregates, confirming osteonecrosis.
Histopathology also revealed fibrinoid necrosis of vascular walls and lumen occlusion beneath the mucosa, suggesting a vasculitic process.
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) of the alveolar process and adjacent mucous membrane detected Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV), directly linking the HZ infection to the affected osteonecrotic tissue.
Patient had no history of other common causes of osteonecrosis of the jaw (tumors, radiotherapy, antiangiogenic agents, antiresorptive drugs).

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Patient had no previous history of therapy with antiangiogenic agents or antiresorptive drugs such as bisphosphonates and denosumab.
Patient had no previous history of local radiotherapy.

remaining_uncertainties: Specific diagnostic tests (e.g., Tzanck smear, PCR for VZV) performed to confirm the initial HZ diagnosis by the stomatologist were not documented.
